title: Blood Distribution to Body Regions
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter traces blood from the aorta to each body region and back to the heart: the aortic branches and their vertebral levels, the arterial supply of the brain and limbs, and venous return through the venae cavae and the hepatic portal system. It then turns to physiology, explaining why border zones between arterial territories infarct first when pressure falls and why each organ receives the share of cardiac output it does and extracts as much oxygen as it does. Board questions usually describe a weak pulse, a dilated vein, a stroke deficit, or an organ injured in shock and ask for the vessel, level, or mechanism.
prerequisites: Embryonic pharyngeal arch arteries and the foregut, midgut, and hindgut (CV-1, GI-1)
Wall structure of elastic arteries, muscular arteries, arterioles, and veins (CV-2)
Vertebral levels and surface landmarks of the thorax and abdomen
Oxygen content of blood: about 20 mL O2 per 100 mL of arterial blood
Flow, pressure, and resistance in series and parallel circuits (CV-11)

connections.how: The coronary arteries are the first aortic branches, and the heart's near-maximal resting extraction means coronary flow must rise with every increase in demand.
Organs are perfused in parallel, so each organ's arteriolar resistance sets its share of cardiac output.

connections.to: Gastrointestinal blood supply and hepatic disease (GI-5, GI-13-C)
connections.how: The gut arteries and portal circulation are developed organ by organ in GI-5, and cirrhosis produces the portal hypertension described here.

connections.to: CNS blood supply and neurological vascular disease (NE-10, NE-20-A)
connections.how: The circle of Willis and cerebral territories predict the deficits of territorial and watershed strokes.
Aneurysms, peripheral arterial disease, embolism, and shock all play out on this vascular map.

terms.def: Flow through anastomotic channels that enlarge when the main route is narrowed or blocked.
An artery whose territory has no effective anastomosis with its neighbors, so occlusion causes infarction of the tissue it supplies.
The ring of arteries at the base of the brain that links the two internal carotid systems with each other and with the vertebrobasilar system.
The veins that carry blood from the gut, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder through a second capillary bed, the liver sinusoids, before it reaches the inferior vena cava.
A site where portal tributaries connect with systemic veins, providing a bypass around the liver when portal pressure rises.
Abnormally high pressure in the portal venous system, usually from increased resistance to flow through or beyond the liver.
Tissue at the far edge of two adjacent arterial territories, supplied by the most distal branches of each and therefore perfused at the lowest pressure.
The ability of an organ to keep its blood flow nearly constant across a range of perfusion pressures by adjusting its own arteriolar resistance.
Arterial minus venous O2 content across an organ, in mL O2 per 100 mL of blood.
The fraction of delivered oxygen a tissue removes: the arteriovenous O2 difference divided by arterial O2 content.
An organ's oxygen consumption equals its blood flow multiplied by its arteriovenous O2 difference.
Diversion of blood from one vascular bed into another through a collateral pathway when the second bed's pressure falls, as in subclavian steal.

sections.title: Branches of the aorta and their vertebral levels

blocks.text: The ascending aorta gives only the right and left coronary arteries (CV-8) and ends at the sternal angle (T4 to T5 disc). The arch passes back over the left lung root, returns to T4, and gives three branches from right to left: the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian arteries. The brachiocephalic trunk divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries. The asymmetry is embryological: the left fourth arch artery forms part of the definitive arch, while the right forms only the proximal right subclavian (CV-1). The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum, so a mass or aneurysm there causes hoarseness. Each common carotid divides at about C4, where the carotid sinus holds baroreceptors.

The descending thoracic aorta (T4 to T12) gives posterior intercostal arteries to spaces 3 to 11 (the first two arise from the costocervical trunk), subcostal arteries, and bronchial, esophageal, and superior phrenic branches. One large anterior segmental medullary artery, usually on the left, reinforces the anterior spinal artery over the lower cord. Dissection, aneurysm, or aortic clamping can interrupt it and infarct the anterior cord: paraplegia and loss of pain and temperature below the lesion, with vibration and position sense spared in the posterior columns.

The aorta passes the diaphragm at T12 and bifurcates at L4, near the umbilicus. Its unpaired anterior branches follow the embryonic gut (detail in GI-5). The pancreatic head and second part of the duodenum, at the foregut and midgut junction, receive both celiac and SMA blood, and the mesodermal spleen is supplied by the celiac trunk because it forms in the dorsal mesogastrium.

blocks.title: Branches of the abdominal aorta
rows: Foregut to the major papilla, liver, spleen
Midgut: distal duodenum to proximal two thirds of transverse colon
Hindgut: distal third of transverse colon to anal canal above the pectinate line
blocks.caption: Levels follow Moore and vary by about half a vertebra. Gonadal arteries arise high because the gonads develop high and descend.

blocks.text: These levels predict findings. The left renal vein and third part of the duodenum pass between the SMA and aorta; loss of retroperitoneal fat narrows that angle and can obstruct the duodenum (SMA syndrome) or compress the vein (C04). A horseshoe kidney ascends until its isthmus catches under the IMA. Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are infrarenal (CV-18-I). Occlusion of the terminal aorta and common iliacs (Leriche syndrome) causes bilateral buttock and thigh claudication, weak femoral pulses, and erectile dysfunction. In adult coarctation, usually just distal to the left subclavian origin, arm pressure is high and femoral pulses are weak and delayed.

blocks.title: Collateral route around an adult coarctation
steps: High pressure in the subclavian artery above the narrowing
Internal thoracic artery descends behind the costal cartilages
Anterior intercostal arteries carry blood around each space
Flow reverses in enlarged, tortuous posterior intercostal arteries
Blood enters the descending aorta below the coarctation
Enlarged intercostals notch inferior rib borders (about ribs 3 to 8)
blocks.caption: Ribs 1 and 2 are spared because their intercostal arteries arise from the costocervical trunk above the narrowing.

sections.title: Arterial supply of the brain and the circle of Willis

blocks.text: The two internal carotid arteries (ICAs) form the anterior circulation, and the two vertebral arteries join as the basilar artery to form the posterior circulation.

The ICA has no neck branches. It crosses the cavernous sinus beside the abducens nerve and gives the ophthalmic artery, so a carotid embolus can cause transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax) as well as stroke. It then gives the posterior communicating artery and divides into the anterior (ACA) and middle cerebral arteries (MCA). The MCA continues the ICA and receives most emboli. Its lenticulostriate branches are thin end arteries leaving a high-pressure trunk at right angles, so chronic hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis, lacunar infarcts, and Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms. The external carotid supplies no brain, but the middle meningeal artery, from its maxillary branch, runs under the pterion (epidural hematoma).

Each vertebral artery, the first subclavian branch, rises through the transverse foramina from C6 to C1, gives the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), and joins its partner at the lower pons. The basilar artery gives the anterior inferior cerebellar (AICA) and superior cerebellar arteries, then the posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs); the oculomotor nerve emerges between the PCA and superior cerebellar artery.

The circle of Willis is formed by the anterior communicating artery, proximal ACAs, terminal ICAs, posterior communicating arteries, and proximal PCAs. It can refill the territory of a slowly occluded ICA, but a complete, symmetric circle exists in only a minority, and it acts only upstream: an embolus in an MCA branch still infarcts because cortical branches connect only through small leptomeningeal anastomoses. Berry aneurysms form at its branch points, about 90% anteriorly, most often at the anterior communicating junction; one at the posterior communicating origin compresses the oculomotor nerve and dilates the pupil early.

blocks.title: Cerebral and brainstem territories
rows: Leg more than arm; incontinence, behavior change
Face and arm more than leg; aphasia (dominant) or neglect (nondominant)
Lateral medulla: vertigo, dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral Horner, ataxia, and face pain and temperature loss; contralateral body pain and temperature loss
Lateral pons: like PICA plus ipsilateral facial weakness and hearing loss, without dysphagia
Hemiparesis, lost position and vibration sense, ipsilateral tongue weakness
Locked-in state with preserved vertical gaze
blocks.caption: Crossed findings (face on one side, body on the other) localize to the brainstem.

blocks.title: Working out a subclavian steal
blocks.text: A 64-year-old smoker becomes dizzy while painting a ceiling with his left arm. His left radial pulse is weak and delayed, and left arm systolic pressure is 30 mmHg lower. Step 1: the interarm difference places a stenosis in the left subclavian artery. Step 2: if it lies proximal to the left vertebral origin, pressure there is below basilar pressure. Step 3: arm exercise dilates arm arterioles and lowers pressure further, so flow reverses down the left vertebral artery, taking blood from the posterior circulation. Step 4: vertigo and imbalance accompany arm claudication. A stenosis distal to the vertebral origin would cause arm claudication alone.

sections.title: Arteries of the upper and lower limbs and the pulse points

blocks.text: Each limb has one trunk that changes name at fixed landmarks, then divides into arteries that rejoin in arches in the hand or foot. A pulse is palpable where an artery lies near the surface over something firm, and palpating in sequence places an obstruction between the last normal pulse and the first weak one.

The subclavian artery passes between the anterior and middle scalenes with the brachial plexus, so a cervical rib can compress both (thoracic outlet syndrome). Scapular anastomoses bypass an axillary block above the subscapular origin but not below it. The posterior circumflex humeral artery travels with the axillary nerve around the surgical neck, and the deep brachial artery with the radial nerve in the radial groove. A supracondylar fracture in a child can injure the brachial artery, and forearm flexor ischemia heals as Volkmann contracture. The connected palmar arches let either the radial or ulnar artery perfuse the hand (Allen test).

In the femoral triangle the order from lateral to medial is nerve, artery, vein, canal. The medial circumflex femoral artery supplies the femoral head, so a displaced intracapsular neck fracture risks avascular necrosis. The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in its fossa and is tethered, so knee dislocation can tear it. At the lower border of popliteus it divides into the anterior tibial artery, which pierces the interosseous membrane, and the posterior tibial artery, which gives the fibular artery. The lateral compartment has no artery of its own; perforating anterior tibial and fibular branches supply it.

blocks.title: Limb landmarks and pulse points
rows: Medial arm or cubital fossa, medial to biceps tendon
Cubital fossa, at about the radial neck
Radial lateral to flexor carpi radialis; ulnar near pisiform, often faint
Inguinal ligament, continuing the external iliac
Midinguinal point, just below the ligament
Deep in fossa, knee flexed; often faint
Lateral to extensor hallucis longus; absent in a few normal adults
blocks.caption: Emboli lodge most often at the common femoral bifurcation.

blocks.text: Peripheral arterial disease (CV-18-I) favors the superficial femoral artery in the adductor canal and the popliteal artery. Claudication appears one level below the narrowing: aortoiliac disease in the buttock and thigh, femoropopliteal disease in the calf. Ankle pressure normally equals or slightly exceeds arm pressure because the pulse wave amplifies distally, so an ankle-brachial index below about 0.9 means pressure is lost across a stenosis.

blocks.predict: The right femoral pulse is weak and the right popliteal and foot pulses are absent; left leg pulses are normal. Where is the obstruction, and which muscles ache first on walking?
blocks.explain: The first abnormal pulse is the femoral, so the block lies upstream in the right common or external iliac artery. Thigh and calf muscles ache on walking, plus the buttock if the common iliac is involved.

sections.title: Venous return: venae cavae, the left renal vein, and the portal system

blocks.text: Veins are richly interconnected, so a blocked vein reroutes blood through normally tiny channels. The brachiocephalic veins unite behind the right first costal cartilage as the superior vena cava (SVC), which receives the azygos vein at about T4. A mediastinal tumor obstructing the SVC swells the face, neck, and arms and distends chest wall veins (SVC syndrome); blood returns through the azygos vein if the block is above its entry, or reverses through the azygos and lumbar veins to the IVC if below.

The inferior vena cava (IVC) forms at L5, ascends right of the aorta, and passes the diaphragm at T8. The right gonadal vein enters the IVC; the left enters the left renal vein at a right angle, and that vein crosses in front of the aorta below the SMA. Compression there (nutcracker phenomenon) causes hematuria and gonadal back pressure, and with the longer left course explains why varicocele is mostly left-sided. A new isolated right varicocele suggests IVC obstruction or a retroperitoneal mass.

Blood from the gut, spleen, and pancreas passes through the liver sinusoids before the IVC, the basis of first-pass metabolism. The splenic and superior mesenteric veins form the portal vein behind the pancreatic neck. The liver receives about a quarter of cardiac output, three quarters of it portal, yet each source supplies about half its oxygen. Portal pressure is about 9 mmHg against near 0 in the hepatic veins, and the valveless portal system transmits any rise in resistance back to the gut and spleen.

Portal hypertension is classified by site: prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (cirrhosis; schistosomiasis, presinusoidal), or posthepatic (Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis). The hepatic venous pressure gradient is normally up to about 5 mmHg; varices form at about 10 mmHg.

blocks.title: Why portal pressure stays high in cirrhosis
steps: Fibrosis, nodules, and stellate cell contraction raise resistance
Nitric oxide and escaped vasodilators dilate splanchnic arterioles
Portal inflow rises against the high resistance
Low effective arterial volume activates RAAS and sympathetic nerves
Kidneys retain Na+ and water, expanding volume
More splanchnic inflow keeps portal pressure high
blocks.caption: Pressure is resistance times inflow; cirrhosis raises both. The same Na+ retention feeds ascites.

blocks.title: Portosystemic anastomoses
blocks.caption: Anorectal varices differ from hemorrhoids, which are not more frequent in portal hypertension. Congestive splenomegaly sequesters platelets.

blocks.predict: Why does portal blood in cirrhosis reach the azygos vein through the esophagus rather than crossing the liver to the IVC?
blocks.explain: The resistance lies within the liver, so blood takes the low-resistance portosystemic routes upstream; the left gastric vein connects with esophageal veins draining to the azygos, which dilate into varices.
blocks.check: Compare with the causes of portal hypertension and the anastomosis table.

sections.title: Watershed zones and why they infarct first in hypotension

blocks.text: A watershed is tissue fed by the last, smallest branches of two neighboring arterial trees. Pressure falls along every tree because each segment has resistance (CV-11), so the border has the lowest perfusion pressure, and its collaterals (leptomeningeal anastomoses, the marginal artery) are too small to rescue either side. Autoregulation normally hides this: cerebral flow stays nearly constant across a mean pressure of about 60 to 150 mmHg. Below that range, flow falls with pressure and the border zones fail first. Chronic hypertension shifts the range upward, so infarction occurs at pressures safe for others.

blocks.title: From hypotension to watershed infarct
steps: Systemic pressure falls (shock, cardiac arrest, surgery)
Arterioles maximally dilated; autoregulation exhausted
Flow falls in proportion to pressure
Distal border zones receive the lowest pressure
Border tissue infarcts while central territories survive
blocks.caption: The same mechanism operates in brain and colon.

blocks.text: Cortical border zones lie between ACA and MCA, a strip over the upper convexity, and between MCA and PCA in the parieto-occipital region; the internal border zone lies in deep white matter. Bilateral ACA-MCA infarction weakens both proximal arms with face, hands, and legs spared (man in a barrel), and bilateral MCA-PCA infarction can cause Balint syndrome features. A severe carotid stenosis lets a modest systemic fall cause ipsilateral watershed infarcts.

In the colon, the splenic flexure (SMA and IMA) and rectosigmoid junction have weak marginal connections, so hypoperfusion causes ischemic colitis with left-sided pain and bloody diarrhea; the rectum has extra internal iliac supply. The mucosa fails first, because countercurrent exchange in the villi leaves the tips hypoxic. Hypoperfusion gives mucosal or mural infarction; transmural infarction follows occlusion.

blocks.title: Regions that fail first in low flow
rows: Farthest from epicardial arteries; perfused mainly in diastole
Low PO2 from vasa recta countercurrent; high transport demand
blocks.caption: Only brain and colon are true boundaries between territories; the others are distal ends of one supply path.

blocks.text: An embolus or thrombus fills one artery's territory, usually on one side. Strip-like infarcts along border zones, often bilateral and in several organs, point to global hypoperfusion.

blocks.predict: After an hour of hypotension from a ruptured aortic aneurysm, a man has bloody stools, bilateral shoulder weakness with normal grip, rising aminotransferases, and rising creatinine. What links these findings?
blocks.explain: Every organ fell below its autoregulatory range at once, so the regions that fail first were injured: colonic border zones, ACA-MCA cortical border zones, centrilobular hepatocytes, and the outer medulla. An embolus would cause one territorial deficit.
blocks.check: Compare with the border zone table.

sections.title: Distribution of resting cardiac output and organ O2 extraction

blocks.text: Systemic organs are perfused in parallel at the same aortic pressure, so each organ's share of cardiac output is set by its own arteriolar resistance (CV-11). Flow does not simply follow oxygen need: the kidneys and gut use blood for filtration and processing, while the heart strips most of its oxygen.

Arterial blood carries about 20 mL O2/dL. By the Fick principle, O2 consumption equals flow times arteriovenous O2 difference; extraction is that difference divided by arterial content. For the whole body, 5 L/min and 5 mL/dL give 250 mL/min, extraction about 25%, and mixed venous saturation about 75% (PO2 about 40 mmHg). Low extraction means reserve; high extraction means more oxygen can come only from more flow.

blocks.title: Resting flow and O2 extraction
blocks.caption: Approximate resting values; learn the ranking.

blocks.text: The kidneys (about 300 g) have the highest flow per gram of any large organ and filter about 20% of their plasma, so their venous blood stays highly saturated, and their O2 use tracks filtered Na+ load. The densely innervated splanchnic bed is the main blood reservoir. Resting muscle has low flow per gram; in exercise flow rises about 20-fold (CV-12). The brain (about 2% of body weight) uses about 20% of resting oxygen, has no oxygen store, and loses consciousness within about 5 to 10 seconds of no flow; its flow is held constant by autoregulation and raised by PCO2, while hyperventilation constricts cerebral arterioles. The heart's coronary sinus blood is only 25 to 30% saturated, so extra demand must be met by metabolic vasodilation (adenosine, nitric oxide), and a fixed stenosis becomes ischemia (CV-8).

blocks.title: Using the Fick principle
blocks.text: Arterial content is 20 mL/dL. Kidney: flow 11 dL/min, venous 18.5 mL/dL; consumption 11 times 1.5 is 16.5 mL/min, extraction 7.5%. Heart: flow 2.25 dL/min, coronary sinus 6 mL/dL; consumption 2.25 times 14 is 31.5 mL/min, extraction 70%. The kidneys get five times the heart's flow but use half its oxygen. If demand doubles, the kidney can double extraction to 15%, but the heart would need 140% extraction, so its flow must double.

blocks.title: Redistribution of cardiac output in hemorrhage
steps: Blood loss lowers arterial pressure
Baroreceptor firing falls; sympathetic output rises
Alpha-1 constriction of skin, splanchnic, renal, and muscle arterioles
Venoconstriction moves reservoir blood toward the heart
Cerebral and coronary arterioles stay dilated under local control
Brain and heart receive a larger share of output
blocks.caption: These beds tolerate a brief fall in flow; prolonged low flow injures them (CV-18-H).

integration.text: Embryology explains the layout: the asymmetric arch comes from selective persistence of pharyngeal arch arteries, the three gut arteries follow the foregut, midgut, and hindgut, and the right-sided IVC forces the left renal and gonadal veins into longer courses. Physiology explains the behavior: parallel perfusion lets each organ set its own flow, the Fick principle shows why low-extraction beds can be constricted in shock while the heart depends on flow, and falling pressure along each arterial tree makes border zones fail first. Atherosclerosis at branch points, cardiac emboli, cirrhosis, and vasculitis act on exactly these vessels, and collateral flow can either protect tissue (circle of Willis, coarctation) or steal from it (subclavian steal).

summary: The arch gives the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian arteries; the carotids bifurcate at about C4.
Abdominal aortic levels: celiac T12, SMA L1, renal about L1, gonadal about L2, IMA L3, bifurcation L4; the gut arteries supply foregut, midgut, and hindgut.
The circle of Willis protects against slow occlusion of an inflow vessel but not against emboli beyond it.
Proximal subclavian stenosis can reverse vertebral flow during arm exercise (subclavian steal).
Limb arteries change names at fixed landmarks, and the first weak pulse in a sequence localizes an obstruction just upstream.
The long left renal vein crosses below the SMA and receives the left gonadal vein, explaining nutcracker compression and left varicocele.
Portal hypertension opens anastomoses at the lower esophagus, umbilicus, anorectal junction, and retroperitoneum.
Below the autoregulatory range, watershed zones (ACA-MCA, MCA-PCA, splenic flexure, rectosigmoid) infarct first.
The kidney extracts little O2 and the heart the most, so extra coronary supply must come from increased flow.
In shock, sympathetic constriction of low-extraction beds shifts output to the brain and heart.

verify: Vertebral levels of aortic branches (celiac T12, SMA L1, renal about L1, gonadal about L2, IMA L3, bifurcation L4) follow Moore; some review books give the renal arteries at L1 to L2 and the bifurcation at L4 to L5. Confirm the values NABNE expects.
The level of the carotid bifurcation is given as about C4 (upper border of the thyroid cartilage); some sources give C3 to C4.

The origin and usual level of the great anterior segmental medullary artery (artery of Adamkiewicz) vary between sources (commonly T9 to T12, range about T8 to L2); confirm whether NABNE expects the eponym.
The proportion of people with a complete, symmetric circle of Willis varies widely among anatomical series; this chapter states only that it is a minority.
Berry aneurysm site frequencies (about 90% in the anterior circulation, most often at the anterior communicating artery) follow Robbins; percentages for individual sites differ between sources.
The proportion of healthy adults without a palpable dorsalis pedis pulse varies between studies; this chapter states only that it is a small proportion.

Hepatic venous pressure gradient thresholds (normal up to about 5 mmHg; varices at about 10 mmHg or more) follow current hepatology consensus and may be beyond Part I scope; portal and hepatic vein pressures of about 9 and 0 mmHg follow Guyton and Hall.
The cerebral autoregulatory range is quoted as about 60 to 140 mmHg in Guyton and Hall and about 50 or 60 to 150 mmHg elsewhere.

Shares of resting cardiac output differ between Guyton and Hall (kidneys about 22%, skeletal muscle about 15%) and other physiology texts (kidneys and resting muscle each up to about 25%). Organ O2 extraction values, especially splanchnic (about 15 to 20%) and resting skeletal muscle, are approximate and vary between sources.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Volkmann ischemic contracture, Leriche syndrome, Balint syndrome, Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm, and nutcracker phenomenon, or only the descriptive terms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: aortic-branches (arch and abdominal aorta with vertebral levels), circle-of-willis (inferior view with feeding and branch vessels), limb-arteries (upper and lower limb trunks with pulse points), and portosystemic-anastomoses (portal tributaries and the four anastomotic sites).
